Nickel Fraunhofer FKIE, Department of Sensor Data and Information Fusion, Neuenahrer Str. 20, 53343 Wachtberg, Germany article info Article history: Received 23 December 2009 Received in revised form 3 May 2010 Accepted 5 May 2010 Available online 13 May 2010 Keywords: Direct position determination Array processing Emitter localization Maximum likelihood estimation abstract This paper investigates the direct position determination (DPD) problem from passive measurements made with a moving antenna array in the case of a time-varying number of emitting sources. We derive the Crame ́ r-Rao bound (CRB) for the estimation problem and find an approximation that is applicable for a large number of observations. We use different DPD approaches to solve the estimation problem. Therein, all source positions are estimated directly from a single cost function that results from fusing all measurements. The considered DPD approaches are based on Capon’s method and the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation. The ML approach offers a superior performance compared to the Capon-type approach, but leads to a high-dimensional optimization. We use the alternating projection technique to solve the high-dimensional optimization by a sequence of low-dimensional optimizations. Finally, we propose an iterative direct detection and position determination (DDPD) approach that combines the aforementioned DPD and the determination of the total number of sources (commonly called detection), because the total number of sources is typically unknown. We present simulation results that demonstrate the performance of the DDPD approach. & 2010 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction Localization of multiple sources using passive sensor arrays is a fundamental task encountered in various fields like wireless communication, radar, sonar, radio astronomy, and seismology. Passive bearings-only localization (BOL) can be realized by multiple sensors, a moving sensor, or both. A moving platform on a known path is the preferable solution in many applications. The sensor is typically airborne e.g. on an aircraft, a helicopter, or a drone. Also of special importance is underwater acoustic localization using hydrophone arrays on a submarine. We consider a scenario with N observations of Q stationary narrowband far-field sources. An array delivers a batch of data snapshots (complex output data vectors) with a sufficiently high data rate, i.e. the scenario is assumed to be stationary during one batch and non-stationary from batch to batch. The traditional approach to solve the localization problem consists of four steps (Fig. 1). After some pre-processing of the sensor data, the directions of arrival (DOAs) of all sources at all measurement points are estimated with a direction finding (DF) algorithm, like the subspace-based multiple signal classification (MUSIC) method. Typically, DF systems report measurements of different origin, e.g. true sources and clutter (false alarms). Then a bearing data association step follows to partition the DOAs into sets of DOAs belonging to the same source. Multiple hypotheses tracking (MHT) is generally accepted as the preferred method for solving the measurement-to-track association problem [2]. In the last step, the DOAs for each source are used to estimate its position with the help of a suitable BOL algorithm, e.g. the bearings can be intersected to determine the emitter Contents lists available at ScienceDirect journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/sigpro Signal Processing ARTICLE IN PRESS 0165-1684/$ - see front matter & 2010 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. doi:10.1016/j.sigpro.2010.05.010 $ The paper has been published in parts on the EUSIPCO 2009 conference [1]. Corresponding author. Fax: + 49 228 856 277. E-mail addresses: marc.oispuu@fkie.fraunhofer.de (M. Oispuu), ulrich.nickel@fkie.fraunhofer.de (U. Nickel). Signal Processing 90 (2010) 3056–3064\n\n\nposition (triangulation). Aspects of the two-dimensional and three-dimensional BOL and bearings-only tracking problem examined in the literature include estimation algorithms, estimation accuracy, and source observability [3]. Recently, some direct position determination (DPD) methods based on the antenna outputs without computing intermediate parameters like DOAs have been proposed (Fig. 2). The basic idea for a subspace-based DPD approach goes back to the pioneering work of Wax and Kailath [4]. They noted that in this way the measurementto-track association step is avoided. Moreover, this kind of approach was used for a multiarray network in order to estimate the positions of multiple sources without explicitly computing DOAs and times of arrival (TOAs) [5]. Maximum likelihood (ML) methods can be found e.g. in [6,7], but they are computationally more demanding in the case of multiple sources. The cyclic DPD algorithm for cyclostationary signals has been introduced in [8]. In a previous work we proposed a subspace-based DPD approach (referred to as subspace data fusion) for a single moving array [9]. Moreover, we have shown that the DPD approach can be extended to estimate the source states (e.g. positions, velocities) [10]. In all these DPD approaches, the parameters of interest are obtained by minimizing a single cost function into which all array data batches enter jointly (Fig. 2). The estimation accuracy of the source state obtained in this way is much better than the traditional localization approach in situations where the variance of DOA estimates deviates from the corresponding Cram  ́er-Rao bound (CRB). However, the methods presented so far only investigate the case where the number of emitting sources is constant. Farina et al. derived the CRB for the general case that the probability of detection is smaller than unity [11]. We extend the results to the case of multiple sources with intermittent emission and adapt them to derive the CRB for the DPD problem. We present two DPD approaches based on Capon’s (CPN) method [12] and deterministic ML [13]. We show that the positioning accuracy of the ML-DPD approach is much better compared to the CPN-DPD approach in situations of a time-varying number of emitting sources, but this approach leads to a high-dimensional optimization problem. We use the alternating projection (AP) technique to solve the highdimensional optimization by a sequence of low-dimensional optimizations similar to results in [14]. The considered DPD approaches require knowledge of the total number of sources, but in practice this number is unknown. We propose an iterative solution that combines the DPD and the determination of the total number of sources. In the area of signal processing this is commonly referred to as detection. This direct detection and position determination (DDPD) approach uses a sequence of statistical tests to decide if the choice of the source number is correct. The basis of the tests is the fact that the optima of the ML-DPD cost function are w2- distributed. We present simulation results that demonstrate the performance of the DDPD approach. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2.1 introduces the concept of emitting/non-emitting sequences, Section 2.2 presents the data model, and Section 2.3 formulates the estimation problem. In Section 2.4 we derive the CRB for the described DPD problem and find an approximation which is applicable for practical purposes. In Section 3.1, we outline the considered DPD approaches, in Section 3.2 we compare the DPD approaches in simulations and investigate the performance of the DPD approaches. In Section 3.3 we propose the novel DDPD approach. The conclusions are given in Section 4. The following notations are used throughout this paper: ð ÞT and ð ÞH denote transpose and Hermitian transpose, respectively; In and 0n denote the n ndimensional identity and zero matrix, respectively; and Ef g denotes the expectation operation. 2. Detection and estimation problem We consider an antenna array composed of M elements mounted on a moving platform and a scenario with Q fixed sources located at xq =(xq,yq,zq)T, q = 1,y,Q, in the far-field of the antenna array. Problem formulation The received data batches depend on the array transfer vectors, which depend on the relative vectors, which themselves depend on the desired source positions. Now, the problem is stated as follows: Estimate all source positions n from all received data batches Z. To solve the DPD problem, the following assumptions are made: A1. Every set of Qn array transfer vectors is linearly independent [15], i.e. the corresponding Qn DOAs are different and Qn o M, n= 1,y,N. A2. The method most commonly referred to for detecting the number of sources was first introduced in [16] and is based on Akaike’s information criterion (AIC) and Rissanen’s minimum description length (MDL) principle. They mentioned that this kind of estimation offers the advantage that the association problem inherent in the traditional method is circumvented. DPD approaches In this section we outline the DPD approaches (Fig. 2) to solve the localization problem with the assumption that the number of sources Q is known. Note that the proposed DPD approaches do not account for the emitting probabilities Pe,q, because they are not sensor parameters like the probability of detection. The considered DPD approaches are based on Capon’s method and ML estimation using a low-dimensional or high-dimensional optimization, respectively. Therein, the source positions are calculated directly in one step from the covariance matrices at all sensor positions. We mention that, alternatively, the corresponding subspace data can be used by a MUSIC-type or SSF-type (subspace fitting) approach [1]. It is well-known that MUSIC gives superior resolution and tends to be power independent in comparison to Capon’s method, but it is important to note that DPD approaches based on the subspaces require the knowledge of the effective number of sources per batch Qn, n =1,y,N, (Assumption A4), while DPD approaches based on the covariance matrices do not need any a priori knowledge about the effective number of emitting sources. 3.1.1. Capon DPD approach (CPN-DPD) This DPD approach uses a Capon-type cost function [12]. The source positions are calculated directly in one step by fusing the covariances of all batches: x^ CPN-DPD 1⁄4 arg mxin N X n1⁄41 aH n ðxÞR^ 1 n anðxÞ, ð29Þ where the array transfer vector (Eq. (6)) is parameterized by the source position x. The cost function shows minima for a proper choice of x, if the covariance matrix of each batch is consistent with to the corresponding array transfer vector. 3.1.2. Maximum likelihood DPD approach (ML-DPD) The ML estimate of all source locations is given by maximizing the likelihood function (18) or minimizing (26) and substituting nn with n. This leads to n^ ML DPD 1⁄4 arg mnin N X n1⁄41 trfP? AnðnÞR^ ng, ð30Þ where the array transfer matrix in (10) is parameterized by the source locations n. This approach is based on the full data covariance matrices and leads to a single optimization in 3Q dimensions. The cost function is highly nonlinear and multimodal. 3.1.3. Alternating projection DPD technique (AP-DPD) The solution of the ML-DPD approach can be found by adapting the DF algorithm based on the alternating projection (AP) technique described in [14]. The iterative AP technique is a simple technique for multidimensional optimization. Therein, at every iteration a minimization is performed w.r.t. a single parameter while all other parameters are held fixed. To solve the DPD problem, we hold all parameters of a single source fixed. Then, the AP-DPD algorithm performs the 3Q-dimensional optimization by optimizing a sequence of 3-dimensional cost functions (Assumption A4). Comparison of the DPD approaches As an illustration, we consider a scenario in which the sensor moves along an arc from ( 0.5, 0.5,0.5)T to (0.5, 0.5,0.5)T km. Two sources are located on the ground at the positions x1 = (0, 0.5,0)T km and x2 = (0,0.5,0)T km (Fig. 5a). In Fig. 5d the coordinates of the first source are fixed and the function over the remaining two variables is plotted. In Fig. 5b, we assume an emitting probability of Pe,1 =Pe,2 = 1. The CPN-DPD cost function displays well-pronounced minima at the true source positions and no further local minima. In the following cases, the emitting probability of the second source is reduced to Pe,2 =0.7. Conclusions We investigated the DPD problem for multiple sources with intermittent emission. Therefore, we derived the deterministic CRB and presented a computationally convenient approximation of the CRB, which is applicable for practical purposes. Furthermore, we proposed DPD approaches based on the data covariance matrices using a low- or high-dimensional optimization. We used the AP technique to solve the high-dimensional optimization by a sequence of low-dimensional optimizations. In simulations, we demonstrated the superior performance of the ML-DPD approach over the CPN-DPD approach. Consequently, the ML-DPD (and AP-DPD) approach offers a tactical advantage for locating sources with intermittent emission. We proposed an iterative DDPD approach to determine the number of sources and the corresponding source locations. We investigated the proposed method in simulations. Note that the approaches can be extended to moving sources. References [1] M. ConclusionsReferences\n\nShow full outline\n\n\n===== FIGURES (7) =====\n\n\nShow 1 more figure\n\n\n===== ABSTRACT =====\n\nThis paper investigates the direct position determination (DPD) problem from passive measurements made with a moving antenna array in the case of a time-varying number of emitting sources. We derive the Cramér-Rao bound (CRB) for the estimation problem and find an approximation that is applicable for a large number of observations. We use different DPD approaches to solve the estimation problem. Therein, all source positions are estimated directly from a single cost function that results from fusing all measurements. The considered DPD approaches are based on Capon's method and the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation. The ML approach offers a superior performance compared to the Capon-type approach, but leads to a high-dimensional optimization. We use the alternating projection technique to solve the high-dimensional optimization by a sequence of low-dimensional optimizations. Finally, we propose an iterative direct detection and position determination (DDPD) approach that combines the aforementioned DPD and the determination of the total number of sources (commonly called detection), because the total number of sources is typically unknown. We present simulation results that demonstrate the performance of the DDPD approach. ===== KEYWORDS =====\n\nDirect position determination; Array processing; Emitter localization; Maximum likelihood estimation\n\n\nPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issue\n\n\n===== 1. INTRODUCTION =====\n\nLocalization of multiple sources using passive sensor arrays is a fundamental task encountered in various fields like wireless communication, radar, sonar, radio astronomy, and seismology. Passive bearings-only localization (BOL) can be realized by multiple sensors, a moving sensor, or both. A moving platform on a known path is the preferable solution in many applications. The sensor is typically airborne e.g. on an aircraft, a helicopter, or a drone. Also of special importance is underwater acoustic localization using hydrophone arrays on a submarine. We consider a scenario with N observations of Q stationary narrowband far-field sources. An array delivers a batch of data snapshots (complex output data vectors) with a sufficiently high data rate, i.e. the scenario is assumed to be stationary during one batch and non-stationary from batch to batch. The traditional approach to solve the localization problem consists of four steps (Fig. 1). After some pre-processing of the sensor data, the directions of arrival (DOAs) of all sources at all measurement points are estimated with a direction finding (DF) algorithm, like the subspace-based multiple signal classification (MUSIC) method. Typically, DF systems report measurements of different origin, e.g. true sources and clutter (false alarms). Then a bearing data association step follows to partition the DOAs into sets of DOAs belonging to the same source. Multiple hypotheses tracking (MHT) is generally accepted as the preferred method for solving the measurement-to-track association problem [2]. In the last step, the DOAs for each source are used to estimate its position with the help of a suitable BOL algorithm, e.g. the bearings can be intersected to determine the emitter position (triangulation).
